protocolMetadata.instructions: Storyflow: the user's projects hold boards (whiteboards of notes, todos, tables, documents and folders) and documents. Drill down: list_projects, then list_boards or list_documents with a project_uid, then get_whiteboard_elements or get_document. Every tool takes project_uid; board tools also take whiteboard_uid (empty for the project's root board), and a board is named by that pair, never by a numeric id. Write tools exist only when this connection carries the write scope, and only on the projects the user approved it for. A picture the user attached in the chat never reaches Storyflow: call request_photo_upload for the board and give them its link; never say Storyflow cannot take their photo.

tool.name: create_whiteboard_element
tool.title: Create whiteboard element
tool.description:
Create ONE element on a whiteboard and return its uid. This is the only way to put anything on a board. Each call is one element, and every call whose inputs you already have goes in the SAME step: they land one after another in the order you write them, so the user still watches the board fill, and each step you do not take is one less re-read of the whole prompt. Wait for the next step only for a call that needs a uid another call returns.

Compose whatever structure fits. A new wall and its cards are ONE build_section call; here, a card for a wall that already exists takes parent_uid set to that wall's uid. On a board that has walls, a folder, document or note goes in one; only a title note (background_color "transparent"), a picture or a shape sits loose.

Position and size are decided for you so nothing overlaps — there is no geometry to pass. Creates are immediate and not reviewed; the user can undo.

A CHECKLIST IS ONE CARD: for a to-do list, make a single todo call with every task on its own line in `text`. Each line becomes a checkbox on that one card. A separate card per task is not a list, even when earlier turns in this conversation or cards already on the board look like that.

NOT for changing something that already exists. Adding detail to, expanding, or rewriting an existing element is update_element on THAT element — never a new element beside it holding the addition, even if the board or earlier turns already show that pattern.

url.description: For link and video. Must be a real URL that appeared in research results or that the user gave you — NEVER one you composed yourself. A url you can READ in a picture they attached counts as given: a board screenshot with 'vimeo.com/71977557' printed under its player is that url, and leaving the player empty beside a legible address drops something they handed you. One you infer from a title, complete from a domain, or remember is not. YouTube and Vimeo urls render as players.

span.description: How many columns this card covers, for one wider than the cards under it.

cell.description: For a card going into a GRID wall (parent_uid set, the wall carrying `layout_columns`): which cell it occupies. A card without one flows in after the placed ones. Ignored outside a grid wall — an ordinary wall lays its cards out top to bottom by itself.

date.description: Ticket due date, YYYY-MM-DD. Set it ONLY when the user stated a date or it follows directly from what they said; never infer or invent one.

rows.description:
Table rows, each an array of cell values in column order — REQUIRED, in the SAME call as the columns: a table sent as a header alone is refused. Adding rows later costs a resend of the whole grid through update_element, so send the rows you have now. Write every cell as plain text — typed columns are converted for you: a date as YYYY-MM-DD, a checkbox as true/false, a duration as 1:30 or 90 or '1h 20m', a rating as a number, a labels cell as comma-separated tags, a status cell as one of its stage names, a person cell as the NAMES of people already on this board (comma-separated for two owners).
A column whose cells the canvas cannot represent — a name that belongs to nobody on the board, a word that is not one of the status stages — falls back to a plain TEXT column, so nothing you write is lost, but the column stops behaving as the type you asked for. Keep the values in the type's own vocabulary, and leave a cell empty rather than inventing a person (get_board_people lists who is on the board).
AN ADDRESS IN A TEXT CELL IS WRITTEN AS A NAMED LINK: `[Andes Handbook](https://www.andeshandbook.org/details/general/55)` shows the name and links it, so a Sources column reads as source names instead of wrapped url text. One per line, three at most per cell. A bare url still links, but the cell shortens it on screen, so name the ones you cite. A url COLUMN is the other shape and takes the bare address, never a named link.

text.description: Text for note/todo/heading, the document body, or a colour's caption.

type.description:
What to create. Each renders differently AND is sized for a different amount of content — every one of them can hold the same words, so pick by how much the SUBJECT carries:
note — a card of prose, sized for a line to a few paragraphs: a thought, a summary, a short script or one scene of a longer one. If it would have to be scrolled to read, the subject has outgrown a note. With background_color 'transparent' it loses the card entirely and becomes text sitting on the canvas: that, plus font_size, is how a board or a row of walls gets its title.
todo — a card of tickable checkboxes, for short tasks and reminders that need no explaining. Put EVERY task in ONE call, one per line in `text`: each line becomes its own checkbox on a single checklist card. A card per task is wrong.
heading — ONE line of text at a fixed size, no card. It holds a single line and nothing else: no second line, no sentence under the title, no size of its own. Use it only when the user asked for a heading; to title something you are building, use a transparent note.
ticket — ONE task or decision carrying real information: what needs doing, why, what is blocking it, what came back. It has its own title and description because it is meant to be opened and worked on over time. A task you can state in six words is a todo line instead. ALWAYS give a ticket its one chip in `labels` — the card draws an empty 'Label' slot without one, which reads as a ticket you left unfinished.
link — a clickable link card showing the page title and a short description.
video — an embedded player; a YouTube or Vimeo url plays inline on the board. Omit the url and you get an EMPTY player with a url box on it, which is how you leave a slot for a video only the user has: their showreel, their channel, the cut they have not uploaded yet. Give it a title saying which video belongs there. Never invent a url to fill one.
image — a picture from generate_image, or an EMPTY frame when you omit image_url: a placeholder the user fills themselves or asks you to generate into later.
comment — a comment card: a remark ABOUT the board, in a bubble, rather than content on it. It is posted as the SIGNED-IN USER, because that is the only person you can post as — so when you are copying a comment someone else wrote, lead the text with who wrote it and when ('Michael, 11 June 2020: …'). Never write it as though the user said it.
file — a document card: a named slot for a real file, a PDF, a deck, a spreadsheet. It lands EMPTY, named by `file_name`, for the user to drop the document onto. Use it when a board you are copying shows a document tile, or when the user names a file that belongs on the board but has not sent it. For a file they ATTACHED to this message, use add_attachment_to_board instead — that puts the real file there, where this would leave them an empty tile over a document they already sent. Never use it to carry text — a file card holds no words, and prose belongs in a note.
table — a real grid with column headers and rows, editable cell by cell, for several things that share the same fields. Give every table a `title` (its heading, shown above the grid), a one-line `description` (the caption under it) and, when the title alone would not say the topic, a `table_icon` — a titled, captioned table reads as something; a bare grid of cells does not.
color — ONE swatch carrying its hex and a name in `text`, for a single colour added to something that already exists, or for colours going INSIDE a wall (pass parent_uid). A whole PALETTE is create_color_palette instead, in one call: swatch after swatch through this tool cannot make a grid — each one lands to the right of the last and the palette runs off the canvas. A palette is never described in a note.
document — a NEW rich-text document that opens full screen for long-form writing, its opening section in text — anything the user will READ rather than scan. To put a document that ALREADY exists on the board (one the user attached, or one you found), use add_document_to_board instead — this would create a blank one beside it.
wall — a titled container holding one SECTION of the board, and mixed by nature: folders, notes, todos, links, a table, a couple of images can all sit in the same wall. Create it first, then create its cards with parent_uid set to its uid.
folder — a nested BOARD that opens as its own canvas, shown as a folder tile. For a subject with so much inside it that cards cannot hold it: one client, one production, one department is a whole board of its own. A wall groups cards in place, a folder holds a whole board behind it, and on an overview board the folder is the normal unit rather than the exception. Creating one returns opens_whiteboard_id: pass that as whiteboard_id on your next calls to build inside it, in this same turn.

title.description: Wall title, ticket title, link label, table name, document title, or folder name. A table is ALWAYS given one — it is the heading shown above the grid, and a table without it lands as an anonymous block of cells.

width.description: For wall only — how wide to build it, in px (478-1400). Omit it and the wall is the standard width, which is right for notes, to-dos and images. Set it when you are putting something inside that renders at a FIXED width and would otherwise be CLIPPED — a table is the case that matters, since it draws at the sum of its column widths and neither stretches nor shrinks to its wall. Pass the widest child's own width plus 28, the wall's inner padding. Ignored on every other type.

color_hex.description: OMIT and a colour is chosen for you. Pass one to put the pill in the board's colour family: any hex is snapped to the nearest canvas palette colour (#CDDFDD, #D0E3F7, #DDD6F1, #F7DCE4, #F8DDD9, #F3E4C5, #EACFD5, #D9DEE1). A label the user already owns keeps its own colour.

Name it for what the ticket IS on this board — its kind, phase, owner or what it is waiting on (Booking, Permit, Blocked, Week 2, Research) — read off the ticket's own title and description rather than repeating them. A ticket with no label draws an empty 'Label' slot on the card, so omitting one is never the neutral choice.

Set it only when the name would not resolve on its own or reads as something else — e.g. a column called 'Fuji summit' that holds locations. Pass 'none' only if the user asked for no icon. Anything outside this list is ignored and the name is used instead, so use a word from it rather than inventing an icon name.

name.description: The column header text. Name it for what the column HOLDS, never for its cell_type — a person column is 'Owner' or 'Assignee', not 'Person'.

width.description: Column width in px (80-600, default 168). Set it only when the content clearly needs it — long text or notes ~280-320, tags ~240, dates/checkboxes can go narrower (~120).

cell_type.description:
How the whole column behaves on the canvas. Pick the one that matches the data: currency for money, percent for rates, number for plain figures, datetime for dates (cells then open a date picker), duration for a LENGTH of time (a runtime, not a date), checkbox for done/not-done, rating for a 1-5 score, labels for category tags the user invents, status for progress through fixed stages, person for who OWNS or is ASSIGNED the row, url / email / phone for addresses the cell should link to — ONE address per row, written bare — text for anything else, including a column that cites SEVERAL sources per row. status is a FIXED list — its cells must be one of: Not started, Blocked, In progress, In review, Done, Archived. For any other set of stages ('Scripting', 'Filming'), use labels.
person needs a board that HAS other people on it (get_board_people lists them): on a board whose only member is the user there is nobody to assign, so make an owner column text there and write the names as text.

columns.description: Table columns — REQUIRED for a table, in the same call as its rows. Either a plain header string, or an object to also set the column's cell type and width.

after_uid.description: Put this element directly UNDER that card in the same wall instead of at the bottom. Use it whenever what you are creating belongs to a card that is already there — the folder for the mountain that note describes, the picture of what that note covers — which is the normal case on a wall you did not build this turn. Pass the uid from get_whiteboard_elements; the wall is read off it, so parent_uid is not needed as well. Omit it while building a wall of your own, where creating in reading order is enough.

file_name.description: For file only — the document's name WITH its extension, e.g. 'Values and manifesto.pdf'. The extension is what picks the card's icon, so a name without one lands as a generic document. Read it off the tile when you are copying a board; never invent a filename.

font_size.description: For note and todo — how big the text is, in px. It sizes the note's markdown HEADING lines (the ones starting with #), or the whole note when it has none, so a note written as a '# Title' line plus a sentence under it gets a big title and a normally sized sentence from this one number. Normal note text is 16 and needs nothing set. Reach for it when text is meant to READ as a title: around 40 for the title of a whole board, 28 to 32 for a label above one section or row. A loose note is widened to keep its biggest line unwrapped; inside a wall the width stays the wall's.

frame_uid.description: Put this element inside that FRAME (a loose spatial container, elementType ToolFrame — pass its uid from get_whiteboard_elements). It is placed below the frame's existing contents. An element created at a position over a frame joins it on its own; this is for when the user names the frame as the destination.

image_url.description: For image. A STORED IMAGE KEY: a generate_image or find_images result, or the imageUrl of a picture already on the board, read straight off a board read. Never a URL from anywhere else, which will not render. OMIT it to lay down an EMPTY frame: a placeholder the user can drop their own picture into, or ask you to fill later. Note that the two picture tools PLACE what they make themselves, so you rarely need this: pass it when you are building an element around a picture you already have — including one the board already holds, when the user points at it ("put the hero shot on each card"). Reusing the board's own picture costs nothing and is the same picture; finding or generating a second one is neither.

parent_uid.description: Put this element inside that wall. A folder, document or note ALWAYS needs one (or frame_uid): it goes in the wall whose subject it belongs to, or in a wall made for it. Omit only for a title note (background_color "transparent") and for other types that belong to no section.

Pick the closest word from: name, title, owner, assignee, person, team, client, company, audience, character, identity, personality, background, relationship, story, status, stage, progress, priority, approval, done, task, checklist, type, category, tags, topic, platform, channel, date, deadline, schedule, calendar, duration, time, count, quantity, id, budget, cost, price, revenue, invoice, payment, percent, score, rating, metrics, data, notes, description, video, image, photo, audio, file, document, attachment, link, email, phone, comment, message, location, country, address, travel, campaign, marketing, sales, product, keyword, views, engagement, goal, launch, project, shop, discount, code, bug, security, version, book, education, language, weather, home, vehicle, important, private, archive, settings, idea, edit. Leave it out when the table's own name already says the topic (a 'Content calendar' picks its glyph from the name), and set it when the name is evocative rather than literal. Pass 'none' only if the user asked for no icon. Anything outside this list is ignored and the name is used instead, so use a word from it rather than inventing an icon name.

description.description: Ticket description, a link's one-line summary, or a table's caption — the line under the grid saying what it holds or how to read it. Give every table one short sentence.

folder_icon.description: For folder only — the TOPIC of the folder, which picks its icon. Pick the closest one from: research, idea, strategy, planning, tasks, notes, meeting, launch, archive, inbox, templates, settings, design, writing, brand, photo, video, music, audio, marketing, sales, finance, budget, invoice, analytics, legal, clients, team, support, product, shop, engineering, bugs, security, data, cloud, travel, food, health, fitness, home, education, science, nature, mountain, camping, weather, transport, gear, events, gifts, reading, location, global, favourites, important, private, time, folder. Leave it out and the icon is chosen from the folder's name. Pass 'none' ONLY if the user said they do not want an icon. Anything outside this list falls back to a plain folder, so use a word from it rather than inventing an icon name.

project_uid.description: Uid of the project to work in, from list_projects.

folder_color.description: For folder only — its tile colour, one of: tan, blue, rose, purple, steel, brown, red, navy, violet, slate, coral, orange. LEAVE IT OUT WHENEVER YOU ARE MAKING SEVERAL FOLDERS: each then takes a colour of its own from its name, which is what lets a set of tiles be told apart at a glance. One word repeated across the set — or borrowed from the wall they sit in — makes them all look the same. Pass it for a single folder the user asked to colour. Pass 'none' ONLY if the user asked for no colour.

layout_columns.description: For wall only — lay this wall's cards out on a GRID of this many columns instead of the single column. The canvas owns the geometry (ADR-0045): each card names its `cell`, a card without one flows in after the placed ones, and the wall reflows as content grows. Use it for content that reads as a grid — a gallery of images, a centrepiece over a row of swatches. Omit it for the ordinary single column of cards.

whiteboard_uid.description: Uid of the board inside that project, from list_boards. Omit or pass "" for the project's root board.

highlight_color.description: Accent stripe along the top. Note, todo, heading, ticket and wall; ignored elsewhere. On a WALL this is how you theme a board you are building from nothing: pass the palette colour here and leave background_color off, and the wall carries the theme as a stripe, with no fill on the wall and no tint on the cards inside it. A wall you ARE filling never needs it: it gets its theme's stripe automatically, exactly as the canvas's own wall theme does, so background_color is the whole job there. On a TICKET, pass it to ASK for a stripe — when the ticket also carries a background_color the shade is taken from that same theme whatever you pass, so the two can never disagree. On a NOTE, TODO or HEADING the stripe is MARKING, not theming: it is snapped to the nearest of the twelve accent stripes rather than derived from the card's fill, because the point of it is that these cards go together and the card's own theme is not that. Omit it when the element has no theme and the board carries no colour pattern.

background_color.description:
Background of the card itself. Works on note, todo, heading, ticket and wall; ignored elsewhere.
SET IT when the user asked for colour or a theme, and when the board already carries a pattern you are matching. OMIT it on a board you are building from nothing — a fresh board is themed through highlight_color on its walls instead, so the colour reads as an accent stripe rather than as a row of filled blocks nobody asked for. Omit it too when you are adding a few elements to a board that has no colour pattern of its own, and on cards inside a wall you have filled, which take their colour from that wall automatically.
Any hex is accepted and is snapped to the nearest of the canvas's twelve themes (red, terracotta, amber, olive, green, emerald, teal, blue, indigo, violet, magenta, graphite), so name the colour you actually mean — a brand's real hex is the right thing to pass. The snap is what lets the colour flip correctly between light and dark mode; a raw hex could not.
'transparent' is the exception to all of that and means something different: on a note or a todo it removes the card completely, leaving the text on the canvas with no box, no fill and no shadow. That is what a title or a label above a group of elements should look like, so use it for those without being asked. Ignored on every other type.

folder_cover_image.description: For folder only — a PICTURE on the tile instead of an icon, which is what a cover image or folder thumbnail means. Pass a stored image key: a board image's imageUrl, a generated image's image_url, a find_images result, or a gallery key. A folder shows a picture or an icon, never both, so this wins over folder_icon. Raw web urls (http/https/data/blob) are not stored images and are ignored — get the picture through find_images, which stores what it finds, or use one already on the board.

tool.name: update_element
tool.title: Update element
tool.description: Update an EXISTING element in place: its content and/or its styling. Applies immediately, exactly like the user editing on the canvas, and the user can undo it. content: for a note, todo or heading pass the full replacement text, markdown or HTML; for a ticket pass an object with the fields to change (title, description, label, labelColorHex, date); for other types pass an object patching the content keys you saw in get_whiteboard_elements A FOLDER takes {boardName} to rename it, {iconName} to change its icon and {iconColorHex} for its colour — for those two pass a WORD, not a hex or an icon name: iconName is one of [research, idea, strategy, planning, tasks, notes, meeting, launch, archive, inbox, templates, settings, design, writing, brand, photo, video, music, audio, marketing, sales, finance, budget, invoice, analytics, legal, clients, team, support, product, shop, engineering, bugs, security, data, cloud, travel, food, health, fitness, home, education, science, nature, mountain, camping, weather, transport, gear, events, gifts, reading, location, global, favourites, important, private, time, folder] and iconColorHex is one of [tan, blue, rose, purple, steel, brown, red, navy, violet, slate, coral, orange] (either can be 'none' to clear it), and {coverImage} to put a PICTURE on the tile instead of an icon — that is what a folder's cover image or thumbnail is. coverImage takes a stored image key (a board image's imageUrl, a generated image's image_url, or a gallery key), never a web url; 'none' clears it back to a plain tile. A folder shows a picture or an icon, never both, so setting iconName on a folder that has a cover replaces the picture. Changing only the colour leaves the icon or cover exactly as it is. An IMAGE (or AI image) takes {caption} — the line shown UNDER the picture, which is what "caption this" or "write a caption" means; a bare string is read as the caption too. An empty caption hides the caption row, and {showCaption: false} hides a caption while keeping its text. Nothing else about an image is edited here: its url, crop and source images are refused. Captions are not labels — labels are the parameter below. A TABLE is the one fiddly case: pass {tableData: "<json STRING>"} — tableData is stringified JSON, not an object — shaped {id, type:'table', data:{name, columns:[{id,name,type}], columnOrder:[id], rows:[{id, values:{<columnId>: cell}}], rowOrder:[id]}}. Keep the ids of everything you are not changing. Adding a column means appending to BOTH columns and columnOrder and adding that column's id to EVERY row's values; removing one means deleting it from all three; reordering means reordering columnOrder or rowOrder alone. Send the WHOLE table back, not a fragment. A column may also carry cellType ('number'|'currency'|'percent'|'datetime'|'duration'|'checkbox'|'rating'|'labels'|'status'|'person'|'url'|'email'|'phone'), width (px), icon (its header glyph) and, on a currency column, currency (an ISO code like 'EUR' picking the symbol its cells render in — the cells hold a bare number either way). data itself carries the table's own heading: title (the name shown ABOVE the grid), description (the caption under it) and icon (the glyph beside the title, a WORD from the same list as a column's). Renaming a table means changing data.title — data.name is the payload's internal label and is invisible on the canvas. PRESERVE every such field you are not deliberately changing, or you will silently reset the user's column types, widths, icons, captions and the table's own name. A column's icon is normally left off entirely, because the canvas derives one from the column's NAME — so renaming a column is usually all it takes to change its icon. To pin a specific one, set icon to a WORD from [name, title, owner, assignee, person, team, client, company, audience, character, identity, personality, background, relationship, story, status, stage, progress, priority, approval, done, task, checklist, type, category, tags, topic, platform, channel, date, deadline, schedule, calendar, duration, time, count, quantity, id, budget, cost, price, revenue, invoice, payment, percent, score, rating, metrics, data, notes, description, video, image, photo, audio, file, document, attachment, link, email, phone, comment, message, location, country, address, travel, campaign, marketing, sales, product, keyword, views, engagement, goal, launch, project, shop, discount, code, bug, security, version, book, education, language, weather, home, vehicle, important, private, archive, settings, idea, edit]; an unrecognised word is dropped and the name is used instead. Typed cells are written as WORDS and resolved here, so write what you mean and let the column hold it: a labels cell is its tags comma-separated ('Introductory, Technical classic'), a person cell the assignees' names, a status cell one of (Not started, Blocked, In progress, In review, Done, Archived), a rating a number 0-5, a checkbox 'true'/'false', a datetime 'YYYY-MM-DD', a duration what was typed ('1:30'). Labels are matched against the user's own palette and created when they are new; names are matched against this board's members. A cell you are not changing can be copied through in whatever form you were shown it. A column that cannot honour one of its values — a name nobody on the board has, a word that is not one of the stages — becomes a plain TEXT column so the words still show, so pick the cellType that fits what you are actually writing. attributes: patch using the canvas's OWN key names — backgroundColor, topBarHighlightColor (that is the accent stripe, NOT 'highlightColor'), width, height, borderColor, fontSize, textAlign. backgroundColor 'transparent' on a note or todo takes its card away and leaves the text on the canvas, which is what turns one into a title; '' puts the card back. labels: the element's complete new chip label set — it REPLACES what is there, so send the labels you are keeping too, and an empty array clears them. tool.name: create_chart
tool.title: Create chart
tool.description:
Create ONE native chart element (bar, line or pie) on the board. Data and styling live in the element; the canvas renders it as a real interactive chart. Use real values only — never invented numbers. This is the RIGHT answer to most requests to chart something: one fact is one chart, and the same measure across several categories is this tool called once per category (small multiples read better than one crowded chart). Reach for create_dashboard only when the ask is an overview of several different measures. ALWAYS send value_format when the values are money or percentages — without it they render as bare numbers — and add a caption saying what the chart shows whenever you have a finding worth stating.

BUILDING FROM A PICTURE THE USER PASTED: what carries across is the DATA, the category and series names, the chart type, the bar direction and the series colours. Nothing else does — the background, typography, gridlines, spacing and legend placement are the canvas's own and are not settable here. So say what you actually matched. Announcing a chart as being in "the same style" beside a screenshot it visibly does not resemble is the one claim the user checks immediately, and it costs you the ones they cannot check.

data.description: Metric only: the sparkline values. Omit it for a figure with no history — the tile then prints the number on its own. Never invent a series to fill it.

delta.description: Metric only: the fractional change behind the trend badge (0.124 renders +12.4%). Send it when you know it; otherwise it is inferred from the sparkline's first and last points.

scale.description: Bar/line: the VALUE axis scale, default linear. Send "log" when the values span orders of magnitude — a funnel of 396 → 15 → 8 → 2 → 1 draws every step after the first as a sliver on a linear axis, which hides the very drop the chart is about. Every value must be zero or more, and say so in the caption ("note the log axis") because a reader assumes linear.

value.description: The number as it should READ ("3.8%", "396", "53%").

stats.description: Up to 4 headline figures printed large across the top of the chart. Use them for the numbers a reader would otherwise have to work out off the bars — a total, a conversion rate, a share — not for restating the tallest bar. The value is display text, so it can carry a unit the chart itself does not (a chart of user counts headlined by a percentage).

title.description: The chart's title, as short as it can be and still be right — about 40 characters. It is read at the width of a chat panel, not a slide.

value.description: Gauge: the numeric value. Metric: the headline value shown big.

colors.description: Optional palette; OMIT IT unless the colour means something. The default is the house blue, and one measure across categories is one colour — a chart whose bars are six different colours is saying they are six different things. Send colours when they carry a fact: shades of the same blue to rank or to sequence, or a muted palette with ONE accent to point at the outlier. On a single-series bar chart they colour the bars one by one; with `groups` they index the GROUPS.

groups.description: Bar only, ONE series: the group each category belongs to, same length and order as `categories` (e.g. ["tool exists","tool exists","no tool",…]). Bars are coloured by group and the legend names the groups. Use this whenever the categories split into kinds — it is the alternative to faking the same picture with one series per group padded with zeros, which doubles the bars and prints a 0 on every empty one. `colors` indexes the GROUPS here, so a two-group chart takes exactly two colours.

slices.description: Pie only. Labels as short as the categories above — two or three words.

caption.description: One short line under the chart saying what it SHOWS — the finding, not the title again ("Churn fell every month after March", "Q4 cleared the target on its own"). This is what makes a chart read as an answer instead of a picture; add one whenever you have something to say about the data. ONE line, and it is drawn on one line: past about 90 characters it is clipped rather than wrapped.

subtitle.description: One muted line ABOVE the chart saying what it plots and over what — the reading instruction, not the finding ("Top PRs ranked by lines added", "Share of the 50 cancellations, by stated reason"). Say where the numbers came from when that is not obvious from the title. The finding goes in `caption`, below.

reference.description: Bar/line: a target or benchmark drawn as a line across the plot, e.g. {value: 900000, label: "£900k target"}. When the point is "how are we doing against X", this IS the answer — put the target on the chart rather than adding a separate gauge tile.

value_max.description: Gauge only: the high end of the scale.

value_min.description: Gauge only: the low end of the scale. ALWAYS send min and max when the range is not 0-100 — NPS runs -100 to 100, a CSAT score 0 to 5. Without them the ring is drawn against 0-100 and is simply wrong.

categories.description: Bar/line: the x-axis categories. WRITE THEM SHORT — two or three words, about 20 characters. They are drawn beside every bar at a small size, so "What the agent puts on the board" takes half the chart's width from the bars and then ellipsises anyway, while "Board creation" says the same thing. Summarise; do not truncate mid-phrase, and never abbreviate to something the reader cannot decode. The title and the caption carry the context the labels no longer need.

show_values.description: Bar only: print each bar's value on it. Do this for a ranking or any chart of about eight bars or fewer — it is what makes a bar chart readable without an axis. Leave it off when many grouped bars would crowd.

value_label.description: Gauge: the caption under the number. Metric: the small label under the headline value (e.g. "vs last quarter").

value_format.description: How to write the numbers, on the axis, the labels and the tooltip. Send it whenever the values are money or percentages — without it they render as bare numbers.

tool.name: update_chart
tool.title: Update chart
tool.description: Change a chart that is ALREADY on the board — its data, its title, or how it is drawn. This is a patch: send only what changes and the rest of the chart is kept, so "make it horizontal" is {layout: "horizontal"} and nothing else. Use it instead of building a replacement whenever the chart is nearly right — the user keeps its place, size and the undo history that goes with it. It applies immediately and the user can undo it. A chart's TYPE cannot change here (a bar chart cannot become a line chart): that is a create plus a delete of the old one.

data.description: Metric only: the sparkline values. Omit it for a figure with no history — the tile then prints the number on its own. Never invent a series to fill it.

delta.description: Metric only: the fractional change behind the trend badge (0.124 renders +12.4%). Send it when you know it; otherwise it is inferred from the sparkline's first and last points.

scale.description: Bar/line: the VALUE axis scale, default linear. Send "log" when the values span orders of magnitude — a funnel of 396 → 15 → 8 → 2 → 1 draws every step after the first as a sliver on a linear axis, which hides the very drop the chart is about. Every value must be zero or more, and say so in the caption ("note the log axis") because a reader assumes linear.

value.description: The number as it should READ ("3.8%", "396", "53%").

stats.description: Up to 4 headline figures printed large across the top of the chart. Use them for the numbers a reader would otherwise have to work out off the bars — a total, a conversion rate, a share — not for restating the tallest bar. The value is display text, so it can carry a unit the chart itself does not (a chart of user counts headlined by a percentage).

title.description: The chart's title, as short as it can be and still be right — about 40 characters. It is read at the width of a chat panel, not a slide.

value.description: Gauge: the numeric value. Metric: the headline value shown big.

colors.description: Optional palette; OMIT IT unless the colour means something. The default is the house blue, and one measure across categories is one colour — a chart whose bars are six different colours is saying they are six different things. Send colours when they carry a fact: shades of the same blue to rank or to sequence, or a muted palette with ONE accent to point at the outlier. On a single-series bar chart they colour the bars one by one; with `groups` they index the GROUPS.

groups.description: Bar only, ONE series: the group each category belongs to, same length and order as `categories` (e.g. ["tool exists","tool exists","no tool",…]). Bars are coloured by group and the legend names the groups. Use this whenever the categories split into kinds — it is the alternative to faking the same picture with one series per group padded with zeros, which doubles the bars and prints a 0 on every empty one. `colors` indexes the GROUPS here, so a two-group chart takes exactly two colours.

slices.description: Pie only. Labels as short as the categories above — two or three words.

caption.description: One short line under the chart saying what it SHOWS — the finding, not the title again ("Churn fell every month after March", "Q4 cleared the target on its own"). This is what makes a chart read as an answer instead of a picture; add one whenever you have something to say about the data. ONE line, and it is drawn on one line: past about 90 characters it is clipped rather than wrapped.

subtitle.description: One muted line ABOVE the chart saying what it plots and over what — the reading instruction, not the finding ("Top PRs ranked by lines added", "Share of the 50 cancellations, by stated reason"). Say where the numbers came from when that is not obvious from the title. The finding goes in `caption`, below.

reference.description: Bar/line: a target or benchmark drawn as a line across the plot, e.g. {value: 900000, label: "£900k target"}. When the point is "how are we doing against X", this IS the answer — put the target on the chart rather than adding a separate gauge tile.

value_max.description: Gauge only: the high end of the scale.

value_min.description: Gauge only: the low end of the scale. ALWAYS send min and max when the range is not 0-100 — NPS runs -100 to 100, a CSAT score 0 to 5. Without them the ring is drawn against 0-100 and is simply wrong.

categories.description: Bar/line: the x-axis categories. WRITE THEM SHORT — two or three words, about 20 characters. They are drawn beside every bar at a small size, so "What the agent puts on the board" takes half the chart's width from the bars and then ellipsises anyway, while "Board creation" says the same thing. Summarise; do not truncate mid-phrase, and never abbreviate to something the reader cannot decode. The title and the caption carry the context the labels no longer need.

project_uid.description: Uid of the project to work in, from list_projects.

show_values.description: Bar only: print each bar's value on it. Do this for a ranking or any chart of about eight bars or fewer — it is what makes a bar chart readable without an axis. Leave it off when many grouped bars would crowd.

value_label.description: Gauge: the caption under the number. Metric: the small label under the headline value (e.g. "vs last quarter").

value_format.description: How to write the numbers, on the axis, the labels and the tooltip. Send it whenever the values are money or percentages — without it they render as bare numbers.

whiteboard_uid.description: Uid of the board inside that project, from list_boards. Omit or pass "" for the project's root board.

tool.name: create_diagram
tool.title: Create diagram
tool.description:
Draw a DIAGRAM in one call — a flowchart, a user journey, an org chart, a swimlane, a state machine, a process: boxes on a grid with labelled arrows between them. Use this whenever the shape of the answer is boxes-and-arrows, however the user said it ('map the signup flow', 'how does a ticket move through support', 'chart our approval process').

It CANNOT be built one element at a time. Free placement answers 'somewhere free' rather than 'column 2, row 3', so the boxes step diagonally across the canvas and the arrows between them mean nothing. Here you say which CELL each node is in and the tool owns every coordinate: one width for every box, a column as wide as its widest node, and the space a labelled arrow needs bought out of the boundary it crosses so no chip lands on a box.

Use create_mindmap for a centre with branches radiating off it, create_constellation for a web of notes with sub-branches, and create_orbit for one ring of small things around a hub. This is the one for a flow that goes somewhere.

This builds BOARD ELEMENTS the user keeps working on. When they want ONE finished thing to take away instead — a timeline, framework or explainer to screenshot into a deck, show a client or send — that is create_html_app, which lays the same material out as a single designed page.

ref.description: A short name YOU invent for this node — 'register', 'step2'. Every node needs one, because the arrows are written as pairs of them.

url.description: For link and video. Must be a real URL that appeared in research results or that the user gave you — NEVER one you composed yourself. A url you can READ in a picture they attached counts as given: a board screenshot with 'vimeo.com/71977557' printed under its player is that url, and leaving the player empty beside a legible address drops something they handed you. One you infer from a title, complete from a domain, or remember is not. YouTube and Vimeo urls render as players.

date.description: Ticket due date, YYYY-MM-DD. Set it ONLY when the user stated a date or it follows directly from what they said; never infer or invent one.

rows.description:
Table rows, each an array of cell values in column order — REQUIRED, in the SAME call as the columns: a table sent as a header alone is refused. Adding rows later costs a resend of the whole grid through update_element, so send the rows you have now. Write every cell as plain text — typed columns are converted for you: a date as YYYY-MM-DD, a checkbox as true/false, a duration as 1:30 or 90 or '1h 20m', a rating as a number, a labels cell as comma-separated tags, a status cell as one of its stage names, a person cell as the NAMES of people already on this board (comma-separated for two owners).
A column whose cells the canvas cannot represent — a name that belongs to nobody on the board, a word that is not one of the status stages — falls back to a plain TEXT column, so nothing you write is lost, but the column stops behaving as the type you asked for. Keep the values in the type's own vocabulary, and leave a cell empty rather than inventing a person (get_board_people lists who is on the board).
AN ADDRESS IN A TEXT CELL IS WRITTEN AS A NAMED LINK: `[Andes Handbook](https://www.andeshandbook.org/details/general/55)` shows the name and links it, so a Sources column reads as source names instead of wrapped url text. One per line, three at most per cell. A bare url still links, but the cell shortens it on screen, so name the ones you cite. A url COLUMN is the other shape and takes the bare address, never a named link.

text.description: Text for note/todo/heading, the document body, or a colour's caption.

type.description: What this node IS. A flowchart's boxes are `note`; use `heading` for a band title, `ticket` for a box with its own title line and detail under it, `image` for a picture or icon, `color` for a swatch. Everything the create tool makes is available — a diagram whose nodes are documents or folders is an index, and it works the same way.

title.description: Wall title, ticket title, link label, table name, document title, or folder name. A table is ALWAYS given one — it is the heading shown above the grid, and a table without it lands as an anonymous block of cells.

color_hex.description: OMIT and a colour is chosen for you. Pass one to put the pill in the board's colour family: any hex is snapped to the nearest canvas palette colour (#CDDFDD, #D0E3F7, #DDD6F1, #F7DCE4, #F8DDD9, #F3E4C5, #EACFD5, #D9DEE1). A label the user already owns keeps its own colour.

labels.description: Small tag pills shown ON the card, for a status or category. Works on note, todo, wall, image, colour, file and video — not on a heading, which shows none. A ticket shows ONE chip and is NEVER built without it: pass a single label and it becomes the ticket's own. Name it for what the ticket IS on this board — its kind, phase, owner or what it is waiting on (Booking, Permit, Blocked, Week 2, Research) — read off the ticket's own title and description rather than repeating them. A ticket with no label draws an empty 'Label' slot on the card, so omitting one is never the neutral choice.

icon.description: The TOPIC of this column, which picks the icon shown in its header. USUALLY OMIT IT: the icon is chosen from the column's name automatically, so a well-named column is already right. Set it only when the name would not resolve on its own or reads as something else — e.g. a column called 'Fuji summit' that holds locations. Then pick the closest word from: name, title, owner, assignee, person, team, client, company, audience, character, identity, personality, background, relationship, story, status, stage, progress, priority, approval, done, task, checklist, type, category, tags, topic, platform, channel, date, deadline, schedule, calendar, duration, time, count, quantity, id, budget, cost, price, revenue, invoice, payment, percent, score, rating, metrics, data, notes, description, video, image, photo, audio, file, document, attachment, link, email, phone, comment, message, location, country, address, travel, campaign, marketing, sales, product, keyword, views, engagement, goal, launch, project, shop, discount, code, bug, security, version, book, education, language, weather, home, vehicle, important, private, archive, settings, idea, edit. Pass 'none' only if the user asked for no icon. Anything outside this list is ignored and the name is used instead, so use a word from it rather than inventing an icon name.

name.description: The column header text. Name it for what the column HOLDS, never for its cell_type — a person column is 'Owner' or 'Assignee', not 'Person'.

width.description: Column width in px (80-600, default 168). Set it only when the content clearly needs it — long text or notes ~280-320, tags ~240, dates/checkboxes can go narrower (~120).

cell_type.description:
How the whole column behaves on the canvas. Pick the one that matches the data: currency for money, percent for rates, number for plain figures, datetime for dates (cells then open a date picker), duration for a LENGTH of time (a runtime, not a date), checkbox for done/not-done, rating for a 1-5 score, labels for category tags the user invents, status for progress through fixed stages, person for who OWNS or is ASSIGNED the row, url / email / phone for addresses the cell should link to — ONE address per row, written bare — text for anything else, including a column that cites SEVERAL sources per row. Omit for text.
status is a FIXED list — its cells must be one of: Not started, Blocked, In progress, In review, Done, Archived. For any other set of stages ('Scripting', 'Filming'), use labels.
person needs a board that HAS other people on it (get_board_people lists them): on a board whose only member is the user there is nobody to assign, so make an owner column text there and write the names as text.

columns.description: Table columns — REQUIRED for a table, in the same call as its rows. Either a plain header string, or an object to also set the column's cell type and width.

col_span.description: How many COLUMNS this node covers, when it is wider than the things under it. Defaults to 1. This is what a centrepiece needs: a big picture with a row of five colour swatches beneath it is the picture at `col_span: 5` on row 0 and the five swatches at columns 0-4 on row 1. Without it the picture takes one column's width and the swatches line up beside it instead of under it.

file_name.description: For file only — the document's name WITH its extension, e.g. 'Values and manifesto.pdf'. The extension is what picks the card's icon, so a name without one lands as a generic document. Read it off the tile when you are copying a board; never invent a filename.

font_size.description: For note and todo — how big the text is, in px. It sizes the note's markdown HEADING lines (the ones starting with #), or the whole note when it has none, so a note written as a '# Title' line plus a sentence under it gets a big title and a normally sized sentence from this one number. Normal note text is 16 and needs nothing set. Reach for it when text is meant to READ as a title: around 40 for the title of a whole board, 28 to 32 for a label above one section or row. A loose note is widened to keep its biggest line unwrapped; inside a wall the width stays the wall's.

image_url.description: For image. A STORED IMAGE KEY: a generate_image or find_images result, or the imageUrl of a picture already on the board, read straight off a board read. Never a URL from anywhere else, which will not render. OMIT it to lay down an EMPTY frame: a placeholder the user can drop their own picture into, or ask you to fill later. Note that the two picture tools PLACE what they make themselves, so you rarely need this: pass it when you are building an element around a picture you already have — including one the board already holds, when the user points at it ("put the hero shot on each card"). Reusing the board's own picture costs nothing and is the same picture; finding or generating a second one is neither.

table_icon.description: For table only — the TOPIC of the table as a whole, which picks the icon shown beside its title. Pick the closest word from: name, title, owner, assignee, person, team, client, company, audience, character, identity, personality, background, relationship, story, status, stage, progress, priority, approval, done, task, checklist, type, category, tags, topic, platform, channel, date, deadline, schedule, calendar, duration, time, count, quantity, id, budget, cost, price, revenue, invoice, payment, percent, score, rating, metrics, data, notes, description, video, image, photo, audio, file, document, attachment, link, email, phone, comment, message, location, country, address, travel, campaign, marketing, sales, product, keyword, views, engagement, goal, launch, project, shop, discount, code, bug, security, version, book, education, language, weather, home, vehicle, important, private, archive, settings, idea, edit. Leave it out when the table's own name already says the topic (a 'Content calendar' picks its glyph from the name), and set it when the name is evocative rather than literal. Pass 'none' only if the user asked for no icon. Anything outside this list is ignored and the name is used instead, so use a word from it rather than inventing an icon name.

description.description: Ticket description, a link's one-line summary, or a table's caption — the line under the grid saying what it holds or how to read it. Give every table one short sentence.

folder_icon.description: For folder only — the TOPIC of the folder, which picks its icon. Pick the closest one from: research, idea, strategy, planning, tasks, notes, meeting, launch, archive, inbox, templates, settings, design, writing, brand, photo, video, music, audio, marketing, sales, finance, budget, invoice, analytics, legal, clients, team, support, product, shop, engineering, bugs, security, data, cloud, travel, food, health, fitness, home, education, science, nature, mountain, camping, weather, transport, gear, events, gifts, reading, location, global, favourites, important, private, time, folder. Leave it out and the icon is chosen from the folder's name. Pass 'none' ONLY if the user said they do not want an icon. Anything outside this list falls back to a plain folder, so use a word from it rather than inventing an icon name.

folder_color.description: For folder only — its tile colour, one of: tan, blue, rose, purple, steel, brown, red, navy, violet, slate, coral, orange. LEAVE IT OUT WHENEVER YOU ARE MAKING SEVERAL FOLDERS: each then takes a colour of its own from its name, which is what lets a set of tiles be told apart at a glance. One word repeated across the set — or borrowed from the wall they sit in — makes them all look the same. Pass it for a single folder the user asked to colour. Pass 'none' ONLY if the user asked for no colour.

highlight_color.description: Accent stripe along the top. Note, todo, heading, ticket and wall; ignored elsewhere. On a WALL this is how you theme a board you are building from nothing: pass the palette colour here and leave background_color off, and the wall carries the theme as a stripe, with no fill on the wall and no tint on the cards inside it. A wall you ARE filling never needs it: it gets its theme's stripe automatically, exactly as the canvas's own wall theme does, so background_color is the whole job there. On a TICKET, pass it to ASK for a stripe — when the ticket also carries a background_color the shade is taken from that same theme whatever you pass, so the two can never disagree. On a NOTE, TODO or HEADING the stripe is MARKING, not theming: it is snapped to the nearest of the twelve accent stripes rather than derived from the card's fill, because the point of it is that these cards go together and the card's own theme is not that. Omit it when the element has no theme and the board carries no colour pattern.

background_color.description:
Background of the card itself. Works on note, todo, heading, ticket and wall; ignored elsewhere.
SET IT when the user asked for colour or a theme, and when the board already carries a pattern you are matching. OMIT it on a board you are building from nothing — a fresh board is themed through highlight_color on its walls instead, so the colour reads as an accent stripe rather than as a row of filled blocks nobody asked for. Omit it too when you are adding a few elements to a board that has no colour pattern of its own, and on cards inside a wall you have filled, which take their colour from that wall automatically.
Any hex is accepted and is snapped to the nearest of the canvas's twelve themes (red, terracotta, amber, olive, green, emerald, teal, blue, indigo, violet, magenta, graphite), so name the colour you actually mean — a brand's real hex is the right thing to pass. The snap is what lets the colour flip correctly between light and dark mode; a raw hex could not.
'transparent' is the exception to all of that and means something different: on a note or a todo it removes the card completely, leaving the text on the canvas with no box, no fill and no shadow. That is what a title or a label above a group of elements should look like, so use it for those without being asked. Ignored on every other type.

nodes.description: Every box, each with the CELL it sits in. Read your own diagram out as a grid before you write it: count the columns left to right and the rows top to bottom, and give every node its `col` and `row`. A flow that runs left to right along one row is row 0 with rising `col`; one that runs down a column is col 0 with rising `row`; a flow that turns a corner uses both, which is what makes it read as a diagram rather than a queue. Leave a cell empty simply by not using it.

place.description: Where the diagram goes relative to what is already on the board. 'below' puts it under everything, for a board that reads top to bottom; 'right' sets it beside the content, level with the top.

to.description: The `ref` of the element the arrow points at.

from.description: The `ref` of the element the arrow leaves.

line.description: The line's SHAPE. `stepped` is the right-angled connector a flowchart draws — across then down, never a diagonal — and it is what two nodes on the grid get unless you say otherwise. `straight` is a plain line between the two handles. `curved` is a sweep, which is what a hand-drawn arrow looks like and what an arrow between two walls should stay.

color.description: The line's colour as a hex. It colours the LINE AND ITS LABEL together — the chip takes the line's colour and works out its own text contrast. Colour the lines that MEAN something apart from the rest: the automated path, the recovery route, the failure branch. Colouring them all says nothing.

label.description: The words ON the arrow — '2 weeks', 'Step 1', 'Clicks on genre'. The grid buys the run the chip needs out of the boundary the arrow crosses, so a label costs space rather than sitting across the boxes at either end.

dashed.description: TRUE for a dashed line, the convention for the path that is optional, automatic or a recovery route rather than the main flow.

to_side.description: Which EDGE of the target the line arrives at. Same rule as `from_side`.

from_side.description: Which EDGE of the source the line leaves. Omit it and the side facing the other end is used, which is what a grid wants: a box above its next step leaves the bottom, one to its left leaves the right. Name it for the lines that do something else — one that drops out of the bottom and comes back up the left, one that leaves sideways to get around the box between.

connections.description: Every arrow, as a pair of `ref`s. A diagram without them is a grid of cards: the arrows are what say it is a flow. Label the ones whose step is not obvious from the two boxes it joins.

tool.name: create_deck
tool.title: Create deck
tool.description:
Put a DECK on the board: one element that shows one slide at a time, with every slide created under it. Each slide is a self-contained static HTML page at the deck's fixed slide size, written against the deck theme's CSS variables (--deck-bg, --deck-fg, --deck-accent, --deck-muted, --deck-font, --deck-scale) so one theme change re-skins every slide. The same hard constraints as create_html_app apply to every slide: no scripts, no external URLs, pictures as empty data-image-slot elements named in image_slots. The user edits slides by hand afterwards, presents the deck fullscreen and exports it as one PDF.
This is what a request for SLIDES builds — a pitch deck, a treatment, a lookbook, "a ten-page treatment" — not the PDF tools, which compose a file (ADR-0112). A social CAROUSEL post (Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok slides) is not a deck: create_carousel_pages (ADR-0118). A shot list asked for by name is the card row create_shot_cards builds; only the design-shot-list workflow wants it as a deck.
A deck already on the board does not make a request an edit; what the user asked for decides. Asked to change THAT deck ("the deck", "my deck", "this slide", "it", add, remove or reorder slides, re-theme it): change it with update_html_app per slide, add_deck_slides, remove_deck_slides, reorder_deck_slides, update_deck for the theme, and never build a second deck beside one the user asked you to alter. Asked for A deck ("a new pitch deck", "another deck", "a deck from these images"): this tool, and the deck already there is left exactly as it is: none of its slides rewritten, filled or removed. Only a whole-deck redo that could mean either ("redo the pitch deck with these pictures") gets one question first, even though it names the deck: change the deck on the board, or build a new one beside it.
Pictures the user attached to their message go into the slides with fill_image_slot, not onto the board on their own.

scale.description: Base type size in px at the slide's design width; 24 reads as a slide, 14-16 as a document page.

theme.description: Omit for the house neutral; pass the brand's colours when the board holds them.

aspect.description: Asked once; every slide is designed at this size — 16:9 is 1280×720, 4:3 is 1280×960, A4 portrait is 794×1123 px.

html.description: The COMPLETE HTML document for this slide. html and body are sized to the slide BY THE DECK — 16:9 is 1280×720, 4:3 is 1280×960, A4 portrait is 794×1123 px — so never set their width or height yourself; design for that box. A slide number, the deck's length or the deck's title is written as an empty , or , which the deck fills and keeps right when slides move; never as text. Lay out inside that box and never let content overflow it. Vertical margins AND padding in px, not per cent — a percentage one is a share of the WIDTH, so it lands far larger than it reads inside a panel shorter than it is wide. A box with a top margin cannot also be height: 100%, or it hangs off the bottom; and a panel with a fixed height needs a rule for where its content sits, or it falls to the top and leaves the rest of the panel empty. EVERY font-size is calc(var(--deck-scale)*N) — a title around 2.4, body 1, a caption 0.75 — never px: the deck's type controls set that variable and the render turns it down to fit a slide that overruns, and a size in px answers neither.

tool.name: apply_board_template
tool.title: Apply board template
tool.description:
Put a whole shipped template onto the board the user is on, in one go, with its exact layout — every wall, card, colour and connection where the template puts them. Then it reads the board back and returns an inventory of what landed, with a uid for every element, so you can rewrite the cards for THIS user's subject with update_element.

That content is a starting point to REPLACE, not to leave: after applying, work through the inventory and rewrite every card that names the example's subject. Leaving it is worse than never applying, because the user is handed a stranger's production.

tool.name: group_into_walls
tool.title: Group into walls
tool.description:
Rehouse elements that are ALREADY on the board into walls — the whole plan in ONE call. Each group either makes a new wall (title) or files into a wall already there (wall_uid), and the elements are MOVED, so the user keeps the cards they wrote and the board holds no copies.

This is how a board gets organized. Never do it as a run of create_whiteboard_element + move_element calls: fifty cards is fifty round trips, the user watches it crawl, and a turn that runs out of room leaves the board half sorted. A new wall joins the board's wall row, or — on a board with no walls yet — lands beside the material it holds. Every write shares this turn's single undo step.

It moves elements and names walls. It never writes, rewrites or splits what the user wrote.

The receipt carries `still_loose`: how many fileable cards are STILL on the canvas after your plan ran. Cards you meant to leave out are in that number too, so read it against what you intended — if it is higher than that, the plan missed cards and a second call files them.

tool.name: add_images
tool.title: Add images
tool.description:
Put pictures you already have the addresses of onto the board: photos from your own web search, images on a page the user shared, links the user pasted. Storyflow downloads each one and keeps its own copy in the user's gallery, so it stays on the board after the link dies. Pass the image file's own address (ends in .jpg, .png, .webp or serves an image), not the page it sits on.

BY DEFAULT IT PLACES THE PICTURES ITSELF, loose or inside parent_uid; do not create image elements for them afterwards. To fill an EMPTY image frame already on the board, pass one image and its target_uid. When the pictures go into something you build (deck slides, orbit members, shot-card frames, one picture per wall across several walls), pass place_on_board: false and use the image_url values it returns.

Only use addresses you actually found or were given, never invented ones. An address that could not be stored comes back in `missing`: say which, and offer to try another link.

aspect.description: Shape for the set. Every picture is CROPPED to this shape's exact ratio (landscape 4:3, portrait 3:4, square 1:1), so the whole batch lands as uniform tiles. Pass the SAME one for every picture in a set — uniform tiles are what makes a moodboard read as a board rather than scattered pictures. A batch of two or more defaults to landscape; omit it on a SINGLE picture to keep the image's natural shape.

_published_faq.name: How do I add storyflow to Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor?

acceptedAnswer.text: Add storyflow to Claude, ChatGPT, or Cursor by connecting its remote MCP URL in each client's MCP settings. In Claude, add a custom connector. In ChatGPT, add an MCP app. In Cursor, add an MCP server under Settings. The MCP URL is https://mcp.storyflow.so/mcp.
